title: Harshita Brella's Family Flew 4,000 Miles to Britain. They Are Still Waiting for Justice.
excerpt: Eighteen months after a young Indian bride was found dead in a London car boot, her parents' UK visit exposes the structural failures that leave South Asian migrant women at risk
body:
## 4,000 Miles for Answers

Eighteen months after Harshita Brella's body was found in the boot of a car in Ilford, east London, her family has done what they say British authorities have failed to do: cross an ocean to demand justice. In May 2026, Harshita's parents and brother flew from New Delhi to the United Kingdom for the first time in their lives — not to sightsee, but to retrace their daughter's final days and hold the system that failed her to account.

Harshita, a 24-year-old from Delhi who had moved to Corby, Northamptonshire, after her marriage, was found dead in November 2024. Her husband, Pankaj Lamba, has been charged with her murder, along with additional charges of rape and sexual assault. He remains at large — 18 months on, one of Britain's most wanted fugitives.

## A System That Looked Away

What makes the Brella case so devastating is not merely its violence but the cascade of institutional failures that preceded it. Harshita had reportedly made complaints about domestic abuse before her death. Advocates say those complaints were not escalated, not investigated with urgency, and not treated as the life-threatening emergency they were.

The family's UK visit has been structured as part campaign, part pilgrimage. They held a prayer meeting in Corby, visited the site where Harshita lived, and met with legal advisers to explore options for pressing British authorities on the investigation's pace. They have also called on the Indian government to push for Lamba's extradition, should he be located on Indian soil.

"We are not here for sympathy," Harshita's father told reporters. "We are here because our daughter trusted this country, and this country owes her justice."

## The Migrant Women's Gap

Harshita's story has become a flashpoint in a broader conversation about the vulnerability of South Asian women who migrate to the UK through marriage. Domestic violence charities have long warned that spousal visa holders face a structural trap: their immigration status is often tied to their partner, creating a power asymmetry that abusers exploit.

Southall Black Sisters, one of Britain's oldest South Asian women's organisations, has documented hundreds of cases in which migrant women were unable to leave abusive marriages because doing so would jeopardise their right to remain in the country. The so-called "no recourse to public funds" condition attached to many spousal visas means that even women who do leave often cannot access shelters, benefits, or legal aid.

In Harshita's case, advocates argue that the system not only failed to protect her but may have inadvertently isolated her further. Her family, thousands of miles away in Delhi, had limited visibility into her daily life. The cultural expectation that marital difficulties should be resolved privately — what researchers call the "honour burden" — may have delayed her seeking help.

## A Diaspora Reckoning

For Britain's 1.8-million-strong Indian diaspora community, the Brella case has prompted uncomfortable introspection. Community leaders have called for better support networks for newly arrived brides, including mandatory welfare checks and multilingual helplines. A Change.org petition launched in Harshita's name, demanding resettlement rights for families of homicide victims, has gathered momentum.

The case also raises pointed questions about transnational policing. Pankaj Lamba is believed to have fled Britain shortly after Harshita's death. Whether he is in India, a third country, or still hiding in the UK remains unclear. The Indian High Commission in London has said it is cooperating with British police, but the family's frustration with the pace of that cooperation is palpable.

## Justice Deferred

The Brella family's visit to Britain is, in one sense, an act of defiance: a refusal to let their daughter's death become a cold case. In another, it is a damning indictment of the systems — legal, diplomatic, and communal — that were supposed to protect a young woman who left home for a new life.

Harshita Brella trusted that marriage would bring her safety and opportunity in Britain. Eighteen months after her death, her family is still waiting for the country she chose to prove it deserved that trust.

*Sources: BBC News; Rayo UK; Sky News; Southall Black Sisters; Pravasi Samwad; Change.org petition.*
